questionText: `class VendingMachine { enum State { NO_COIN, HAS_COIN, DISPENSING, SOLD_OUT } private State state = State.NO_COIN; void insertCoin(){ if(state == State.NO_COIN){ System.out.println("Coin accepted"); state = State.HAS_COIN; } else if(state == State.HAS_COIN){ System.out.println("Coin already inserted"); } else if(state == State.SOLD_OUT){ System.out.println("Machine is sold out, coin rejected"); } else if(state == State.DISPENSING){ System.out.println("Please wait, dispensing in progress"); } } }` -- selectItem() and dispense() would each repeat a similar chain. What's the core structural problem this demonstrates?
option1: Every method (insertCoin(), and presumably selectItem(), dispense()) has to independently re-check the same state field with its own full if-else chain, so the total number of branches grows with (number of states) times (number of actions), and every new state requires editing every existing method
option2: The enum State should be replaced with a String to fix this
option3: This code will not compile since enums cannot be compared with ==
option4: The problem is that insertCoin() is a void method instead of returning a boolean
correctOptionExplanation: Same anti-pattern as the MediaPlayer example, now in vending-machine form -- branches multiply across states times actions.

questionText: `interface VendingState { void insertCoin(VendingMachine machine); void selectItem(VendingMachine machine); void dispense(VendingMachine machine); } class VendingMachine { private VendingState state = new NoCoinState(); void setState(VendingState state){ this.state = state; } void insertCoin(){ state.insertCoin(this); } void selectItem(){ state.selectItem(this); } void dispense(){ state.dispense(this); } }`. Which class is the Context and which represents the State abstraction?
option1: VendingMachine is a concrete state; VendingState is the context
option2: Both VendingMachine and VendingState are contexts
option3: VendingMachine is the Context -- it holds the current state reference and forwards every action to it; VendingState is the shared contract every concrete state (NoCoinState, HasCoinState, etc.) must implement
option4: VendingMachine is the abstraction; VendingState is a concrete implementation of it
correctOptionExplanation: VendingMachine owns the reference and delegates; VendingState is the interface every concrete condition implements.

questionText: `interface AtmState { void insertCard(Atm atm); void enterPin(Atm atm); void ejectCard(Atm atm); } class IdleState implements AtmState { public void insertCard(Atm atm){ System.out.println("Card accepted"); atm.setState(new CardInsertedState()); } public void enterPin(Atm atm){ System.out.println("Insert a card first"); } public void ejectCard(Atm atm){ System.out.println("No card to eject"); } } class CardInsertedState implements AtmState { public void insertCard(Atm atm){ System.out.println("Card already inserted"); } public void enterPin(Atm atm){ System.out.println("PIN verified"); atm.setState(new AuthenticatedState()); } public void ejectCard(Atm atm){ System.out.println("Ejecting card"); atm.setState(new IdleState()); } }`. Atm starts in IdleState. This sequence runs: atm.insertCard(); atm.ejectCard(); atm.enterPin();. What prints for the third call?
option1: "PIN verified"
option2: "Insert a card first" -- after ejectCard() returned the ATM to IdleState, calling enterPin() now runs IdleState.enterPin(), not CardInsertedState.enterPin()
option3: "Card already inserted"
option4: Nothing prints, the program throws an exception
correctOptionExplanation: Tracing the transitions: insertCard moves Idle to CardInserted, ejectCard moves it back to Idle, so enterPin() runs on IdleState.

questionText: You said: "the classes themselves are affecting the context class, which was not happening in Strategy Pattern." Is this accurate, and what's the precise mechanism?
option1: Not accurate -- Strategy Pattern also lets concrete strategies swap themselves out on the context
option2: Not accurate -- in State Pattern, only the context itself is ever allowed to call setState(), concrete states never do
option3: Accurate, but only because State Pattern uses abstract classes instead of interfaces
option4: Accurate -- a concrete state's method (e.g. CardInsertedState.enterPin()) directly calls atm.setState(new AuthenticatedState()) as part of handling the action, so the currently active state decides and executes the transition itself; in Strategy Pattern, the injected strategy has no equivalent mechanism to swap itself out -- that decision stays with the external client calling setStrategy()
correctOptionExplanation: This confirms and precisely restates the exact distinction being worked out -- states self-transition, strategies do not.

questionText: Beyond who performs the swap, what's the difference in when a swap happens between State and Strategy?
option1: In State Pattern, a swap happens as an automatic, expected consequence of handling a normal action call -- every call to enterPin(), pressPlay(), etc. potentially changes which object is active next. In Strategy Pattern, a swap is a deliberate, separate act the client performs whenever it wants (calling setPaymentStrategy() is not a side effect of calling pay())
option2: In State Pattern, swaps only happen once, at object creation, and never again
option3: In Strategy Pattern, swaps happen automatically inside every method call, exactly like State
option4: There is no timing difference between the two patterns
correctOptionExplanation: State transitions are baked into normal action handling; Strategy swaps are a separate, deliberate client decision.

questionText: `interface SignalState { void next(TrafficLight light); } class RedState implements SignalState { public void next(TrafficLight light){ System.out.println("Red -> Green"); light.setState(new GreenState()); } } class GreenState implements SignalState { public void next(TrafficLight light){ System.out.println("Green -> Yellow"); light.setState(new YellowState()); } } class YellowState implements SignalState { public void next(TrafficLight light){ System.out.println("Yellow -> Red"); light.setState(new RedState()); } } class TrafficLight { private SignalState state = new RedState(); void setState(SignalState state){ this.state = state; } void next(){ state.next(this); } }`. Who decides that Green is followed by Yellow, not straight back to Red?
option1: TrafficLight decides, based on an if-else inside next()
option2: The client calling light.next() decides each time by passing a parameter
option3: GreenState decides, entirely on its own -- its next() method is hardcoded to call light.setState(new YellowState()); TrafficLight has no idea what comes after Green, it just delegates to whichever SignalState is currently active
option4: Java decides automatically based on enum ordinal order
correctOptionExplanation: TrafficLight never contains sequencing logic -- each state hardcodes its own next transition.

questionText: `interface OrderState { void ship(Order order); void cancel(Order order); } class CancelledState implements OrderState { public void ship(Order order){ System.out.println("Cannot ship a cancelled order"); } public void cancel(Order order){ System.out.println("Already cancelled"); } }`. order.ship() is called while in CancelledState. What happens, and is this the right way to handle it?
option1: It throws a checked exception automatically since ship() was called on the wrong state
option2: It prints "Cannot ship a cancelled order" and does nothing else -- no state change, no exception thrown here; this is a valid way to handle an invalid action for a given state, though throwing an exception instead is also a legitimate choice depending on how strict the system needs to be
option3: It silently ships the order anyway since ship() was called
option4: The code fails to compile since CancelledState doesn't implement a ship() that changes state
correctOptionExplanation: Not every action needs to cause a transition or throw -- handling it as a no-op with a message is a valid design choice.

questionText: `interface OrderState { void pay(Order order); void cancel(Order order); } class PendingState implements OrderState { public void pay(Order order){ boolean success = tryPayment(); if(success){ System.out.println("Payment successful"); order.setState(new PaidState()); } else { System.out.println("Payment failed"); order.setState(new PaymentFailedState()); } } public void cancel(Order order){ System.out.println("Order cancelled before payment"); order.setState(new CancelledState()); } }`. Adding PaymentFailedState here only required editing the body of one existing method, PendingState.pay(). Do PaidState and CancelledState need any changes at all for this new state to exist?
option1: Yes, every existing state must add a new method to detect payment failure
option2: Yes, the OrderState interface must gain a new method that PaidState and CancelledState both need to implement
option3: No, but only because PaymentFailedState is declared as abstract
option4: No -- PaidState and CancelledState are completely untouched; only PendingState.pay() needed one new branch inside it, since that's the only place the new state can be reached from. This is what actually makes adding a state cheap: a small, localized change to whichever one existing state's method decides to transition into it, not a change that ripples through every existing class
correctOptionExplanation: Adding a state is genuinely cheap only when it's reached from inside an already-existing action method -- here, PendingState.pay() already existed and just gained one more branch. If reaching a new state instead required a brand-new action/method that didn't exist before, that method would have to be added to the interface, and every existing state class would be forced to implement it too -- exactly as expensive as adding a new action.

questionText: The same Document system needs a brand-new action, void requestChanges(Document doc), callable from InReviewState (sends it back to Draft) but meaningless in every other state. What's required to add this?
option1: Add requestChanges() to the DocumentState interface, add a matching delegating method to Document (the context), and implement requestChanges() in EVERY existing concrete state class (DraftState, InReviewState, PublishedState, RejectedState) -- even the ones where it just prints "not applicable" -- because the interface now requires it everywhere
option2: Only InReviewState needs to implement the new method, since that is the only state where it makes sense
option3: Nothing needs to change in the existing state classes, only in Document
option4: This can be added without touching the DocumentState interface at all
correctOptionExplanation: A genuinely new action must be added to the interface, which forces every implementer to provide it -- this is the expensive direction, contrasted with Q8's localized change.

questionText: `interface ElevatorState { void requestFloor(Elevator elevator, int floor); void doorOpen(Elevator elevator); }`. When client code calls elevator.requestFloor(5), what's the actual sequence?
option1: elevator directly moves to floor 5 without consulting any state object
option2: The client must first check elevator.getState() and manually call the right method on it
option3: requestFloor(5) internally calls state.requestFloor(elevator, 5) on whichever ElevatorState is currently held; that state's implementation decides what actually happens and may call elevator.setState(...) if a transition is warranted
option4: requestFloor(5) throws an exception unless the client passes the current state as a parameter
correctOptionExplanation: The context's public method is a thin delegation to whichever state object is currently active.

questionText: IdleState, CardInsertedState, and similar ATM state classes hold no instance fields. Following the same reasoning worked out for MediaPlayer, what's the practical implication?
option1: These classes must be marked final and cannot be extended
option2: A single shared instance of each state class (e.g. one static IdleState object) can safely be reused across every transition and even across multiple separate Atm objects, instead of calling new IdleState() every time a transition happens back to Idle
option3: These classes must be converted into enums to work correctly
option4: Stateless classes cannot implement interfaces in Java
correctOptionExplanation: Stateless implementations can be safely shared as single reusable instances instead of being re-created on every transition.

questionText: Two completely separate ChessGame objects, game1 and game2, both point their state field at the exact same shared InProgressState instance. Is this safe?
option1: No, two different context objects can never point to the same state object
option2: No, this would merge game1 and game2 into a single game
option3: Only safe if game1 and game2 are running one after another, never at the same time
option4: Yes -- InProgressState holds no data of its own, so calling a method on it always just acts on whichever context object was passed in as a parameter; the shared state object itself never remembers anything between calls
correctOptionExplanation: A stateless state object can be referenced by any number of independent context objects simultaneously without any correctness issue.

questionText: Does State Pattern, by itself, stop a developer from writing `RejectedState.approve(Document doc){ doc.setState(new PublishedState()); }` -- letting a rejected document skip straight to published?
option1: No -- nothing in the pattern prevents any concrete state from calling setState() with any other state class; which transitions are valid is purely a matter of what each state's methods are written to do, and the compiler has no concept of a valid transition graph
option2: Yes, Java enforces valid state transitions automatically once you use interfaces
option3: Yes, but only if DocumentState is declared as an abstract class instead of an interface
option4: No transitions are possible without a special TransitionValidator class
correctOptionExplanation: The pattern organizes behavior into classes, but it doesn't enforce which transitions are logically valid -- that discipline is entirely up to the developer.

questionText: CancelledState for an order needs to remember a specific cancellationReason string provided when cancel() was called. What does adding this field change?
option1: Nothing changes, fields can always be added to state classes for free
option2: This is invalid Java -- state classes implementing an interface cannot have fields
option3: Once CancelledState holds data specific to one particular cancellation, that instance is no longer safely shareable across multiple different Order contexts or reusable as a single static instance -- each cancelled Order now needs its own fresh CancelledState carrying its own reason
option4: This requires converting CancelledState from a class into an interface
correctOptionExplanation: The moment a state class holds per-instance data, the shared-instance optimization no longer applies -- it now needs a fresh object per use.

questionText: In a vending machine, should the number of items currently in stock be a field on VendingMachine (the context) or on SoldOutState?
option1: On SoldOutState, since that's the state most related to stock running out
option2: On VendingMachine -- stock count belongs to the specific machine, not to any one state; every state class needs to be able to read it, and putting it on one particular state class would make it inaccessible or duplicated elsewhere
option3: On every state class equally, duplicated across all of them
option4: Stock count cannot be represented in the State Pattern at all
correctOptionExplanation: Data that belongs to the object overall, and that multiple states need to read, lives on the context, not on any single state.

questionText: `class Document { private DocumentState state = new DraftState(); void setState(DocumentState state){ this.state = state; } void submitForReview(){ state.submitForReview(this); } void approve(){ state.approve(this); } void reject(){ state.reject(this); } }`. If a new DraftState were mistakenly written to implement Document instead of DocumentState, what would go wrong?
option1: Nothing, Document and DocumentState are interchangeable in Java
option2: The state field would then hold a reference to itself
option3: This would actually still compile and work correctly
option4: Compile error the moment Document tries to assign new DraftState() to its state field, since state is declared as type DocumentState and DraftState would no longer implement that interface
correctOptionExplanation: The type system enforces that only genuine DocumentState implementations can ever be assigned to the state field.

questionText: private DocumentState state = new DraftState(); sets the initial state as a field initializer. What's an equally valid alternative?
option1: Accept the initial DocumentState as a constructor parameter, e.g. public Document(DocumentState initialState) { this.state = initialState; }, letting the caller control what state a new Document starts in
option2: Initial state can only ever be set as a field initializer, there is no other valid way
option3: The initial state must always be null until the first action is called
option4: Java requires the initial state to be set inside a static block
correctOptionExplanation: Constructor injection of the starting state is an equally valid, sometimes more flexible, way to establish the initial condition.

questionText: A developer writes `HasCoinState.selectItem(VendingMachine machine){ System.out.println("Dispensing item"); }` and forgets to call machine.setState(new DispensingState()). What's the practical consequence?
option1: Java throws a compile error since every state method must call setState()
option2: The machine automatically moves to DispensingState anyway, since the print statement implies it
option3: The machine silently stays in HasCoinState forever after this -- the message prints, but nothing about the tracked state changes, so the next action is still handled as if a coin is just sitting there
option4: This causes a NullPointerException on the next call
correctOptionExplanation: Forgetting the transition call is a real, silent bug class specific to this pattern -- the printed message can mislead you into thinking the transition happened.

questionText: `class Game { enum Phase { WAITING, IN_PROGRESS, FINISHED } private Phase phase = Phase.WAITING; void handleEvent(String event){ switch(phase){ case WAITING: if(event.equals("start")){ phase = Phase.IN_PROGRESS; } break; case IN_PROGRESS: if(event.equals("end")){ phase = Phase.FINISHED; } break; case FINISHED: System.out.println("Game already finished"); break; } } }`. This squeezes all logic into ONE method instead of three. Does that avoid the core problem State Pattern solves?
option1: Yes, since there's only one method now instead of three, the problem is fully solved
option2: No -- the problem was never really 'too many methods,' it was that state-specific logic is scattered inside conditional branches instead of organized into its own unit; this single switch still mixes every phase's behavior together, and every new phase or event still means editing this one already-large method rather than adding an isolated new class
option3: Yes, because switch statements are always better than if-else chains
option4: No, because this code does not compile
correctOptionExplanation: Consolidating into fewer methods doesn't fix the underlying issue -- the logic for every state is still tangled together in one place.

questionText: Looking back at the MediaPlayer Main class from earlier -- did it ever reference PlayingState, PausedState, or StoppedState by name anywhere?
option1: Yes, main() had to explicitly construct the correct state class before each call
option2: Yes, main() had to check getStateName() before every call to know which method was safe to call
option3: It's required to reference them, otherwise the code won't compile
option4: No -- Main only ever called pressPlay(), pressPause(), pressStop() on the MediaPlayer object; it never knew or needed to know which concrete state class was active at any point
correctOptionExplanation: The client is fully decoupled from concrete state classes -- it only ever talks to the context.

questionText: An Order needs to independently track BOTH a payment status (Unpaid/Paid/Refunded) and a shipping status (NotShipped/Shipped/Delivered), which can combine almost any way. Reasonable way to model this?
option1: Give Order two separate state references -- a PaymentState field and a ShippingState field, each with its own interface and concrete classes -- so the two state machines evolve independently instead of cramming every combination into one giant OrderState
option2: This cannot be modeled with State Pattern at all, only with if-else
option3: Use a single OrderState interface with a method for every possible combination of payment and shipping status
option4: Merge payment and shipping into a single field that alternates between the two concerns
correctOptionExplanation: Independent concerns can each get their own orthogonal state machine within the same context, avoiding a combinatorial explosion of combined states.

questionText: Every action on VendingMachine should reject a null or negative coin value before anything else, regardless of current state. Where should this check live?
option1: Duplicated inside every concrete state class's insertCoin() method
option2: Inside the VendingState interface as a default method every state must call manually
option3: Inside VendingMachine's own insertCoin() method, before it delegates to state.insertCoin(this) -- since this check doesn't depend on which state is active, there's nothing to make overridable per-state
option4: Inside a separate CoinValidationState that every machine starts in
correctOptionExplanation: Logic that applies identically to every state belongs directly in the context, not scattered across or hooked into every state class.

questionText: A developer adds this in client code: `if (state instanceof CardInsertedState) { System.out.println("card is in"); }`. What's the problem?
option1: Nothing, this is completely normal usage of the State Pattern
option2: This defeats the point of the pattern -- client code checking concrete state identity with instanceof is back to depending on implementations instead of just calling actions on the context; if this info is genuinely needed, expose it through an explicit method like atm.getStatusMessage() implemented per-state
option3: instanceof cannot be used with interfaces in Java, so this won't compile
option4: This is required because AtmState itself cannot know its own class name
correctOptionExplanation: Type-checking concrete state classes from outside reintroduces exactly the coupling the pattern exists to remove.

questionText: Anywhere in Elevator, VendingMachine, Atm, or Document (the context classes), is there ever a line like if (currentCondition == SOME_VALUE) to figure out the object's current condition before deciding what to do?
option1: Yes, every context class needs at least one such check inside its constructor
option2: Yes, but only inside the setState() method
option3: Only if the context has more than 3 possible states
option4: No -- the context never branches on its own condition anywhere; what condition it is in is represented entirely by which object the state field points to, and delegation is how the right behavior gets picked
correctOptionExplanation: The current condition is represented structurally (which object is referenced), not through any conditional check written by the context.

questionText: All examples so far pass the context as a parameter to every state method (void pressPlay(MediaPlayer player)). An alternative bakes the context into each state's constructor (new PlayingState(player)), then calls plain no-arg methods. Real trade-off?
option1: Passing the context as a method parameter keeps state objects context-agnostic and safely shareable/stateless -- the same instance can be reused across many different contexts, since it never stores a reference to any particular one; baking the context into the constructor ties that state instance permanently to one specific context, so it can no longer be shared
option2: There is no real difference, both approaches behave identically in every case
option3: The constructor-injection version is always faster at runtime
option4: The method-parameter version cannot call setState() on the context at all
correctOptionExplanation: Passing context as a parameter is what preserves the ability to share stateless state instances across multiple contexts.

questionText: A developer adds a private field to DispensingState to cache the last dispensed item name: `class DispensingState implements VendingState { private String lastItem; ... }`. If this same instance is being reused across multiple different VendingMachine objects, what risk does this introduce?
option1: No risk, private fields are always safe regardless of how an object is reused
option2: This would cause a compile error since state classes cannot have private fields
option3: This reintroduces exactly the sharing risk from the earlier stateless-instance discussion -- one VendingMachine's dispensing activity could overwrite lastItem while it's still relevant to another VendingMachine sharing the same DispensingState instance, corrupting both
option4: This makes DispensingState automatically become its own separate class per VendingMachine
correctOptionExplanation: A 'stateless' class quietly gaining instance data is exactly what breaks safe sharing across multiple contexts.

questionText: An interviewer describes: "An order object needs to behave differently depending on whatever stage it's currently at in its lifecycle -- what actions are even allowed changes automatically as it moves from one stage to the next, purely as a result of the actions taken on it so far." Which pattern does this signal, and what's the giveaway phrase?
option1: Strategy -- the phrase "behave differently" always signals Strategy Pattern regardless of context
option2: State -- the giveaway is "what actions are even allowed changes automatically... as a result of the actions taken on it so far," meaning the object's own behavior shifts on its own as a consequence of what has already happened to it -- exactly the self-transitioning lifecycle State Pattern is built for
option3: Builder -- because an "order object" is being described, and Builder is for constructing objects
option4: Template Method -- because "lifecycle" implies a fixed sequence of steps
correctOptionExplanation: The specific signal is self-driven behavioral change over a lifecycle, driven by prior actions -- that phrase is the State Pattern tell.

questionText: `interface DiscountStrategy { double apply(double price); } class Cart { private DiscountStrategy discount; void setDiscount(DiscountStrategy d){ this.discount = d; } double checkout(double price){ return discount.apply(price); } }` versus `interface CartState { void checkout(Cart cart); } class EmptyCartState implements CartState { public void checkout(Cart cart){ System.out.println("Cannot checkout an empty cart"); } } class HasItemsState implements CartState { public void checkout(Cart cart){ System.out.println("Order placed"); cart.setState(new EmptyCartState()); } }`. Which snippet is Strategy and which is State, and what's the tell?
option1: Both snippets are State Pattern, since both have a setX() method on the context
option2: Both snippets are Strategy Pattern, since both delegate to an injected interface
option3: The first snippet is State (discount changes over time); the second is Strategy (checkout behavior varies)
option4: The first snippet is Strategy -- Cart never calls setDiscount() itself, only an external client would swap the discount. The second is State -- HasItemsState.checkout() calls cart.setState(new EmptyCartState()) itself, transitioning the cart as a direct consequence of handling checkout(), with no external client involved in that decision
correctOptionExplanation: The discriminator is exactly who calls the setter -- external client (Strategy) versus the active implementation itself (State).

questionText: An Elevator needs emergencyStop() to work identically and immediately regardless of current state -- always forcing it straight to EmergencyState. Is it acceptable for Elevator.emergencyStop() to call this.setState(new EmergencyState()) directly, instead of delegating to state.emergencyStop(this)?
option1: Yes -- when an action's behavior is genuinely identical no matter the current state, there's nothing state-specific to delegate; the context handling it directly is reasonable and mirrors how universal validation logic belongs in the context, not duplicated across every state
option2: No, every single action must always be delegated to the current state with zero exceptions
option3: No, this would require deleting the ElevatorState interface entirely
option4: Yes, but only if EmergencyState is declared as abstract
correctOptionExplanation: When behavior genuinely doesn't vary by state, there is nothing to gain from forcing a delegation through the state interface.

questionText: Pulling this whole session together -- sharpest, code-behavior-based way to distinguish State from Strategy?
option1: State Pattern always uses enums; Strategy Pattern always uses interfaces
option2: State Pattern is for payment systems; Strategy Pattern is for booking systems
option3: In State Pattern, the currently active implementation calls setState(...) on the context itself, as a normal part of handling an action -- the object drives its own transitions. In Strategy Pattern, the currently active implementation never calls anything like setStrategy() on the context -- swapping only ever happens because external client code decided to call it, completely separately from any single method being executed
option4: State Pattern requires exactly 3 concrete classes; Strategy Pattern allows any number
correctOptionExplanation: This is the core, mechanical distinction the whole session was built around: self-triggered transition versus externally-triggered swap.
